chapters.title: Chapter 4: Lagrange Multipliers: Optimization Under Equality Constraints

lessons.title: Solving the Lagrangian: First-Order Conditions and What the Multiplier Means

children.text: Two questions remain from the interviewer. First, the fifty-stock version: can the Lagrangian actually be solved in closed form for any number of assets, not just two? Second, a question nobody has answered yet: what does the multiplier's actual number mean? This lesson answers both, and the second answer turns out to be one of the most useful ideas in the entire course.

body.text: The Lagrange multiplier is not just an algebra intermediate step. Its value measures exactly how much the optimal objective would change if the constraint were relaxed by one unit, a shadow price on the rule you are being forced to obey.

children.text: Write the minimum variance Lagrangian in vector form, for any number of assets at all, and solve its first-order conditions using matrix algebra instead of scalar algebra. Nothing about the method changes from two assets to two hundred.

body.caption: The Lagrangian, identical in form to the two-asset version, just with vectors of any length.
Setting the gradient with respect to w to zero and solving, using the matrix inverse of Sigma.
Plugging the expression for w back into the budget constraint pins down lambda.
The closed-form minimum variance portfolio, for any number of assets. One matrix inversion, no substitution, no iteration.

body.label: Minimum achievable variance
body.context: A standard companion result: plug w* back into wᵀΣw and it collapses to this single scalar expression.

children.text: Numeric Check: Does This Match Everything Else in the Course?

body.title: Show me the matrix inverse arithmetic

content.caption: The standard 2x2 inverse formula, using the determinant computed back in Chapter 2.
Multiplying the inverse by the ones vector.

body.caption: The matrix formula reproduces the exact weights found by substitution (Chapter 3) and by the scalar Lagrangian (Chapter 4, Lesson 1).

body.text: Three completely different-looking routes, plain calculus with substitution, the scalar Lagrangian, and this matrix formula, all land on w1* = 0.3984, w2* = 0.6016. That agreement is the whole point: the matrix version isn't a different answer for bigger problems, it's the exact same method, written so it scales. Swap in a 50-by-50 covariance matrix and this formula still produces the minimum variance portfolio in one matrix inversion, answering the interviewer's original challenge from the start of this chapter.

children.text: What the Multiplier Actually Means: A Shadow Price
This is the piece every earlier lesson postponed. At the optimal solution, the multiplier equals the rate of change of the optimal objective value with respect to the constraint's target.

body.latex: \lambda^* = \frac{dV^*}{dc} \quad \text{where the constraint is written } g(\mathbf{x}) = c
body.caption: The envelope theorem result: lambda measures the marginal cost, or benefit, of loosening the constraint by a small amount.

children.text: For the budget constraint, wᵀ·1 = c, with c normally fixed at 1, this has a genuinely useful reading: c is exactly how much capital you are required to deploy. Push c above 1, say to 1.05, and you are running the portfolio with 5% leverage. Lambda tells you, to a first approximation, how much extra variance that leverage costs.

body.caption: For this particular problem, the multiplier is always exactly twice the minimum variance itself, a clean, checkable relationship.

stats.label: 2 × V*
stats.context: Predicted lambda, from this lesson's relationship

body.text: Concretely: run this two-stock portfolio at 101% invested, one percentage point of leverage, instead of exactly 100%, and minimum variance rises by roughly lambda times 0.01, about 0.00083, from 0.04134 to roughly 0.04217. That is not an abstract algebra fact. It is a real answer to the question, how much extra risk does one more unit of leverage cost me, read directly off a number that fell out of the optimization as a byproduct.

body.title: Interpret a multiplier
body.question: In a target-return-constrained minimum variance problem, minimize wᵀΣw subject to wᵀμ = R*, the Lagrange multiplier on the return constraint comes out to λ = 0.15. What does this number tell you?
options: Nothing useful; λ is just an algebra intermediate step
Demanding one more unit of expected return would increase the minimum achievable variance by approximately 0.15
The portfolio has a 15% chance of underperforming its benchmark
Exactly 15% of the portfolio must be held in cash
body.explanation: A multiplier measures the marginal change in the optimal objective value per unit change in that constraint's target. Here, it says how much minimum variance rises for each additional unit of required expected return, the exact same shadow-price idea this lesson derived for the budget constraint, just applied to the return target instead.

body.title: Check the leverage cost
body.scenario: A fund's Lagrange multiplier on its long-only budget constraint works out to λ = 0.06 at its current minimum variance solution, where minimum variance itself is 0.03.
body.prompt: The fund is considering running at 105% invested instead of exactly 100%. Using the shadow price interpretation, roughly how much would minimum variance increase? Does the λ = 2V* relationship from this lesson hold for these numbers?
body.modelAnswer: Using the shadow price interpretation, minimum variance increases by roughly λ times the change in the budget level: 0.06 × 0.05 = 0.003, so variance rises from about 0.03 to roughly 0.033. Checking the λ = 2V* relationship: 2 × 0.03 = 0.06, which matches the given λ exactly, so these numbers are internally consistent with the closed-form formula this lesson derived.

cards.definition: w* = Σ⁻¹1 / (1ᵀΣ⁻¹1), valid for any number of assets, derived from the Lagrangian's first-order conditions in matrix form.
V* = 1 / (1ᵀΣ⁻¹1), the portfolio variance achieved at w*.
The economic meaning of a Lagrange multiplier: the rate of change of the optimal objective value per unit change in a constraint's target.
The formal result that λ* = dV*/dc, connecting the multiplier's numeric value to the marginal cost or benefit of relaxing a constraint.

points: The Lagrangian's first-order conditions solve in matrix form for any number of assets: w* = Σ⁻¹1 / (1ᵀΣ⁻¹1), no substitution or iteration required.
This formula reproduces the exact same Reliance-TCS weights found by substitution in Chapter 3 and by the scalar Lagrangian earlier in this chapter, confirming all three methods agree.
A Lagrange multiplier is not just an algebra byproduct. It equals the rate of change of the optimal objective value per unit change in the constraint's target, a shadow price.
For the budget-constrained minimum variance problem, the multiplier equals exactly twice the minimum variance itself, λ* = 2V*, a clean, checkable relationship.
Practically, the multiplier lets you estimate the marginal risk cost of relaxing a constraint, such as adding a small amount of leverage, without re-solving the entire optimization from scratch.
The next lesson applies this exact machinery to the full efficient frontier problem, with two constraints, a target return and the budget rule, active at once.
